prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping allows many neutral atoms to be interrogated without perturbing the clock transition and has brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I keep B051 alone as a one-part prize and I have not changed my preferred configuration since round 1. After reading the full exchange, the case rests on three things that the round-1 statements confirm rather than weaken. First, the physical idea is distinct and clean: choose the lattice wavelength so that the light shift is equal for both clock states, and the trap stops being a systematic effect. That is a different step from the comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012), which dealt with counting optical cycles and with isolating one quantum system. Lindroth's formulation, simultaneous interrogation of many atoms at the magic wavelength, is the right way to say it, and I would put that in the citation and keep the redefinition of the second out of it. Second, the result has been verified the way I trust most: clock-to-clock comparisons between independent laboratories on several continents agree at the 10^-18 level, so the open questions are about novelty and credit, not about whether the measurements are sound. The chair's summary records that every member who addresses performance accepts this. Third, six of eight members put exactly the same two names in their configuration, which is unusual on this list. I do not treat that count as merit, but it means the credit has been examined from several directions without anyone proposing a different pair. I also do not move to a B009 pairing: it is not a scientific judgement I can make from my own area, and it would not repair any of the B051 doubts, it would only add a second part with an unresolved single-name credit.
statement.case_against: The reservations I take seriously are three. The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a matter of judgement, and a reader who sees a continuous line from comb to ion clock to lattice clock will call this a continuation. My answer is the magic-wavelength idea, but I accept it is an argument and not a proof. Second, the priority record for the 2001-2003 lattice proposals (Katori, and Lemonde and colleagues) and for the first operating lattice clocks is something I know only at the level of a theorist working next to these groups, and I would support an outside archival or expert check before the final ballot. If that check showed Ye's contribution to be mainly refinement and records, Katori alone or a different composition would be more defensible, though my reading is that the many-body clock work adds physics (spin-exchange and Fermi-degenerate effects inside the clock), not just engineering. Third, the SI second has not been redefined. I regard that as an application still pending, and the prize should rest on what has been measured and reproduced, but a colleague who wants to wait is not unreasonable.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye is credited for the original invention or only for later accuracy and stability records, and says that if the archive shows refinement, a different composition would be more defensible.
responses.response: I think this is the most important open question on B051 and I share your reading of the rule: the prize is for the original experiment. My own view is that Katori holds the idea and the first realisation, and that Ye's contribution is more than a record, because the strontium clock work at JILA took the concept into regimes (control of collisional and spin-exchange shifts, Fermi-degenerate gases in the lattice, a many-body clock) that the original proposal did not anticipate and that changed what the clock is. That is why I would word the citation around invention and realization and the magic-wavelength mechanism, and not around accuracy records. I do not claim the archival priority is settled, and I would accept an outside check that decides between Katori and Ye or a third name. I would not move to Katori alone on the evidence I have.

responses.point: Lindroth locates the distinct step in simultaneous interrogation of many atoms at the magic wavelength, and asks whether to wait for the redefinition of the second or rely on cross-continent comparisons.
responses.response: I adopt your wording for the citation. On timing, I would not wait. The redefinition is a metrological and political process, and the discovery-side reasons for the prize, namely the lattice that does not perturb the transition and the reproduction at 10^-18 across laboratories, are already established. Waiting would tie the prize to an application the citation should not depend on. I also take your point about sympathy for atomic-physics candidates. I have the same lean on the quantum-technology side, and that is why I am relying on you and Kroll for the priority history and not on my own reading.

responses.point: Pearce prefers B051 together with B009 (Halzen alone), accepts that the single-name IceCube credit is unresolved, and asks me whether I prefer Wallraff or Girvin in a B038 trio.
responses.response: On the second part, I cannot support or oppose it on the science, because astroparticle physics is outside my area, but you and Danielsson both say the single-name credit for Halzen is unresolved, and I would not add a part whose credit has to be settled by an outside report just to make a thematic pair. A one-part B051 prize is also fully consistent with the three-person cap. On B038, I am conflicted and I decline to say which of Wallraff or Girvin belongs in a trio, as that is exactly the allocation I should leave to you and the rest of the committee. If B038 is ever live, I would take no part in the discussion or the vote on it, and I note that nobody on the committee wants it as a lead this year.

responses.point: Danielsson pairs IceCube (Halzen) with lattice clocks and notes that a B009 attribution to one person is hard to defend, and in round 1 he asked me to say why lattice clocks were low in his own ranking, reading them as a precise result rather than an instrument.
responses.response: I agree with your reading that the lattice clock is a result with physical content and not a mere instrument, and I am glad the discussion moved you to include it. On the pairing I land differently from you: you yourself say that B050 or B051 alone could be the cleaner prize, and I find that persuasive. If the committee wants a clue-from-nature part, I would want the Halzen credit settled by an outside expert report first, and I would not make my own B051 position depend on it. I would also not block B009 as a second part if the credit question were resolved.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B050 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), argues that reproducible quantised edge transport and ARPES surface states make it mature and overdue, and asks whether I support B051 or a B050 plus B051 prize if credit is not settled.
responses.response: I accept your argument that a prize does not depend on a device, and I retract the weight I put on the absence of dissipationless applications. My remaining concern with B050 is the one you share: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe, which Molenkamp tested, and the three-dimensional work lies outside the credited names. I would prefer an outside expert opinion on whether Kane, Mele and Molenkamp can be defended before I rank it above B051. I would not combine the two as a pairing, because the three-person cap would be exceeded (five names) and I see no scientific reason to join them. B050 remains my first alternative, and if the credit question is resolved cleanly in your favour I would regard it as a legitimate lead and would not oppose it.

responses.point: Kroll values B051 as a new measurement capability, notes a compact Katori-Ye credit, and flags that Ye also appears on a cold-molecule candidate and that fundamental-physics results so far are limits and not discoveries.
responses.response: I agree that the fundamental-physics results so far are limits, and the citation should therefore stay with the established achievement, trapping at the magic wavelength and the 10^-18 performance, and not claim the constants or dark-matter searches as discoveries. On Ye appearing elsewhere, I do not see it as an obstacle here: this prize would rest on the clock work, and the two-part and three-person limits are not stressed by a one-part prize. I also take your distant mentor-lineage disclosure as proper and I would not ask you to step back from B051.

uncertainties: Whether the archival record for the 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposals and the first lattice clocks supports exactly Katori and Ye, and whether Ye's credit is for invention, for the many-body clock, or only for accuracy records; I would support an outside expert check.
Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; this is a judgement, not a measurement.
Whether B050 can be credited fairly without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and without the three-dimensional topological insulator work; I defer to the condensed-matter members.
Whether the single-name IceCube credit for Halzen (B009) can be defended; I cannot judge this and defer to colleagues in astroparticle physics.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, whose national programme is built on the circuit QED architecture (B038), and I work at Chalmers MC2 with colleagues in that field, including a department-level link to Olsson that she has also disclosed. I would recuse myself from any discussion or decision on B038, and I have therefore not put it in my configuration or my alternatives and have declined to rank its credited names. I have no specific conflict with B051, B050 or B009 that I am aware of, and I hold a general sympathy for quantum-technology candidates that I ask colleagues to challenge.
